title: Chronic Diarrhoea
subject: Medicine
summary: Diarrhoea lasting over four weeks, characterised by frequent loose or watery stools. It can lead to malabsorption, dehydration, and malnutrition. Causes range from infections and inflammatory conditions to malabsorption syndromes and malignancies.

sections.p: Chronic diarrhoea is defined as loose or watery stools occurring more than three times per day for at least four weeks. Diagnosis involves a thorough history, physical examination, and targeted investigations to identify the underlying cause.
b: Duration of symptoms is key: >4 weeks.
Consider stool frequency and consistency.

sections.p: Severity is often assessed by the impact on the patient's well-being and nutritional status. Staging is not universally defined but can be based on the presence of complications like dehydration, malnutrition, or electrolyte imbalances.
b: Mild: Minimal impact on daily life, no dehydration.
Moderate: Some impact on daily life, mild dehydration or weight loss.
Severe: Significant impact, severe dehydration, malnutrition, or electrolyte disturbance.

sections.p: In low-resource settings, infectious causes are common, including parasitic infections (Giardia, Entamoeba histolytica), bacterial overgrowth, and post-infectious syndromes. Malabsorption, such as coeliac disease or HIV-related enteropathy, is also significant. Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and malignancy are less common but important to consider.
b: Infectious: Giardiasis, amoebiasis, cryptosporidiosis, helminths.
Malabsorption: Coeliac disease, HIV-related, tropical sprue.
Inflammatory: Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis.
Iatrogenic: Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea, laxative abuse.
Endocrine: Hyperthyroidism.
Neoplastic: Colorectal cancer.

sections.p: Patients typically present with frequent, loose, or watery stools. Associated symptoms can include abdominal pain, bloating, urgency, tenesmus, weight loss, fatigue, and signs of malabsorption such as steatorrhoea or nutritional deficiencies.
b: Stool characteristics: watery, fatty, bloody, nocturnal.
Associated symptoms: pain, bloating, weight loss, fever.
Systemic signs: anaemia, dehydration, vitamin deficiencies.

t.a: Stool microscopy (ova, cysts, parasites, occult blood)
t.b: To identify infectious causes like Giardia, Entamoeba, helminths, or occult bleeding suggesting inflammation or malignancy.
To detect bacterial infections like Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, or C. difficile.
To differentiate inflammatory causes (high) from non-inflammatory causes (low) of diarrhoea. If unavailable, consider empirical treatment for common infections.
To assess for anaemia (iron deficiency, B12/folate deficiency) and signs of chronic inflammation or infection (leukocytosis).
To assess for dehydration and electrolyte imbalances (hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia).
To screen for coeliac disease, a common cause of malabsorption. If unavailable, consider empirical gluten-free diet trial.
To rule out HIV-associated enteropathy or opportunistic infections.
To visualise the colonic mucosa, identify inflammation (IBD), polyps, or malignancy, and obtain biopsies for histological diagnosis. If unavailable, consider sigmoidoscopy or empirical treatment.

sections.p: Urgent medical attention is needed for severe dehydration, significant weight loss, persistent fever, severe abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, or signs of malnutrition. Complications include electrolyte disturbances, dehydration, malabsorption leading to vitamin deficiencies, and anaemia.
b: Severe dehydration or hypovolaemic shock.
Unexplained significant weight loss.
Rectal bleeding or melaena.
High fever.
Severe abdominal pain.
Signs of severe malnutrition or vitamin deficiency.

sections.p: Management focuses on treating the underlying cause, rehydration, nutritional support, and symptomatic relief. For infections, antiparasitic or antibiotic therapy is used. For malabsorption, dietary modifications (e.g., gluten-free) or supplements are crucial. Symptomatic treatment may include antimotility agents if appropriate.
b: Rehydration: Oral rehydration salts (ORS) or intravenous fluids for severe dehydration.
Nutritional support: High-energy, nutrient-dense diet; vitamin and mineral supplements.
Specific treatment: Antiparasitics (e.g., metronidazole for amoebiasis), antibiotics, gluten-free diet for coeliac disease.
Symptomatic relief: Loperamide for symptom control in non-inflammatory diarrhoea (use with caution).

sections.p: Regular follow-up is essential to monitor response to treatment, nutritional status, and for complications. Prevention involves good hygiene practices to reduce infectious causes, safe food and water, and prompt management of underlying conditions.
b: Monitor weight, hydration, and nutritional markers.
Ensure adherence to dietary or medical treatments.
Promote hand hygiene and safe water/food practices.

sections.p: Acute gastroenteritis, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), and functional diarrhoea can mimic chronic diarrhoea. IBS typically presents with abdominal pain related to defecation and changes in stool frequency or form, but without alarm features.
b: Acute gastroenteritis (duration <4 weeks).
Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
Functional diarrhoea.

sections.p: A normal stool microscopy does not exclude parasitic infection, as shedding can be intermittent. Fecal calprotectin can be falsely elevated in inflammatory bowel disease flares but also in infections. Nutritional markers may be normal early in malabsorption.
b: Intermittent shedding of parasites.
Falsely normal electrolytes in mild dehydration.
Normal stool microscopy in some infections.
Normal nutritional markers early in malabsorption.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe dehydration (e.g., sunken eyes, poor skin turgor, reduced urine output).

faq.q: What is the most common cause of chronic diarrhoea in adults?
faq.a: In many settings, functional diarrhoea or IBS is common, but in low-resource areas, chronic infections and malabsorption syndromes are also very frequent.

faq.q: When should I suspect coeliac disease?
faq.a: Suspect coeliac disease in patients with chronic diarrhoea, malabsorption, weight loss, anaemia, and sometimes extra-intestinal manifestations like dermatitis herpetiformis.

Many causes of chronic diarrhoea are curable or manageable with appropriate treatment, such as infections, coeliac disease, or inflammatory bowel disease. Some functional causes may require long-term management.

exam: A 28-year-old man from a malaria-endemic area presents with chronic diarrhoea, weight loss, and a non-healing perianal fistula. What are your top three differential diagnoses and why? — 1. Crohn's disease: Fistula, chronic diarrhoea, weight loss are classic. 2. HIV-related enteropathy/opportunistic infection: Immunocompromise can cause these symptoms. 3. Chronic parasitic infection (e.g., amoebiasis with complications): Can cause chronic diarrhoea and fistulas.

You are managing a patient with chronic diarrhoea and suspected malabsorption. What is the single most important investigation to rule out a common treatable cause, and what are the key findings? — Coeliac serology (anti-TTG, EMA). Positive results indicate coeliac disease, confirmed by biopsy. Negative results make it less likely but don't entirely exclude it.

A patient has chronic watery diarrhoea, weight loss, and an itchy blistering rash on their elbows. What is this rash called and what condition does it suggest? — Dermatitis herpetiformis. It is strongly associated with coeliac disease.

How would you differentiate between inflammatory and non-inflammatory causes of chronic diarrhoea in a resource-limited setting where faecal calprotectin is unavailable? — History (bloody stools, fever, weight loss suggest inflammatory), examination (tenderness, mass), and response to empirical treatment. Stool microscopy for parasites is crucial.

A patient with chronic diarrhoea has hyponatraemia. What are potential causes related to their diarrhoea? — Excessive free water loss from diarrhoea leading to compensatory ADH release (SIADH-like picture), or direct electrolyte losses from the gut.

Why is loperamide sometimes avoided in chronic diarrhoea? — It can mask underlying inflammatory or infectious processes, potentially worsening the condition or delaying diagnosis. It should not be used in bloody diarrhoea or high fever.

What are the key features of chronic diarrhoea that would prompt you to consider malignancy? — Age >50 years, unexplained weight loss, rectal bleeding, iron deficiency anaemia, change in bowel habit, palpable abdominal mass, or family history of colorectal cancer.
